meta_desc: Step-by-step NCERT Class 12 Determinants Exercise 4.2 solutions on properties of determinants, plus a free 8-question quiz to test your row and column skills.

quiz.title: Properties of Determinants Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on the row and column properties used all through Exercise 4.2. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Class 12 NCERT Determinants Exercise 4.2 — properties of determinants

questions.q: If two rows of a determinant are interchanged, the value of the determinant is:
options: multiplied by the sign of the determinant
unchanged in magnitude but its sign is reversed
questions.explanation: Swapping any two rows (or columns) keeps the magnitude the same but changes the sign of the determinant.

questions.q: If every element of a single column of a determinant is multiplied by k, the new determinant equals:
questions.explanation: A common factor from ONE row or column can be taken outside, so multiplying one column by k multiplies the determinant by k once.

questions.q: A 3×3 determinant has two identical rows. Its value is:
options: equal to the repeated row’s sum
questions.explanation: If two rows (or columns) are identical, swapping them gives the same determinant D, but the swap rule says it becomes −D, so D = −D, hence D = 0.

questions.q: For a 3×3 matrix A, det(A) compared with det(A') (the transpose) is:
questions.explanation: The value of a determinant is unchanged when rows and columns are interchanged, so det(A) = det(A'). This is why every row property has a matching column property.

questions.q: The operation R₁ → R₁ + 3R₂ (adding a multiple of one row to another) changes the determinant by:
questions.explanation: Adding a multiple of one row (or column) to another leaves the determinant unchanged. This is the workhorse operation for creating zeros in Exercise 4.2.

questions.q: If a 3×3 determinant is multiplied throughout, i.e. every one of its rows is multiplied by k, the value becomes:
questions.explanation: Each row multiplied by k contributes one factor of k. For all three rows of a 3×3 determinant that gives k×k×k = k³ times the original.

questions.q: A determinant has an entire row of zeros. Its value is:
options: equal to the other rows added
questions.explanation: Taking the common factor 0 out of the zero row multiplies the determinant by 0, so a determinant with a zero row (or zero column) is always 0.

questions.q: To prove a determinant identity like the one factoring to (x−y)(y−z)(z−x), the most efficient first step is usually to:
options: expand fully along the first row
apply column/row operations such as C₂ → C₂ − C₁ to create zeros or common factors
swap the first and last rows
questions.explanation: Subtracting one column (or row) from another creates a common factor like (x−y) that can be pulled out, turning a messy expansion into a clean factorised proof — the standard technique in Exercise 4.2.

faq.q: What does NCERT Class 12 Determinants Exercise 4.2 cover?
faq.a: Exercise 4.2 is entirely about the properties of determinants: how swapping rows changes the sign, how a common factor comes out of a row or column, why identical rows make a determinant zero, and how to add a multiple of one row to another. You use these to prove identities without full expansion.

faq.q: Which property is used most in Exercise 4.2?
faq.a: The invariance property — that adding a multiple of one row or column to another does not change the value. It lets you create zeros or common factors, so most of the proof-type questions in 4.2 start with an operation like R₁ → R₁ + R₂ + R₃.

faq.q: Why does a determinant with two identical rows equal zero?
faq.a: Swapping the two identical rows must reverse the sign, giving D = −D, which forces D = 0. The same reasoning works for two identical columns, which is why proportional rows or columns also give zero.

faq.q: Do I need to expand every determinant in Exercise 4.2?
faq.a: No, and that is the whole point. The exercise trains you to simplify first using properties, pull out common factors, and reduce to a small expansion or a fully factorised form. Expanding blindly usually leads to long, error-prone algebra.
